subthemes.text:
OVERVIEW

[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant), XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX are citizens of Colombia. They are a family of a wife, husband, and three adult children. The family fears a criminal cartel who tried to recruit the youngest child in November 2018. The family made a complaint to the Fiscalia and the Ombudsman, registered with the Victims Unit and were provided with a protection order. The family claimed refugee protection during a pre-planned trip to Canada in December 2018. The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) found that the determinative issue was state protection. I agree that this is the determinative issue.
DECISION

[2] I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

BACKGROUND

[3] The Appellants resided in a quiet suburb of Medellin. The family suspected that gang members would sometimes pass through the neighbourhood to reach nearby high-crime areas. XXXX was actively involved in young leadership programs in his school and community. He is also a talented XXXX who would perform publicly.

[4] In October 2018 the family planned a vacation to Canada for XXXX 2018. On November 20, 2018, an unknown young man visited the family's home and tried to recruit XXXX to the Los Chivos gang. He refused. The young man said he would return and threatened XXXX not to tell his parents. The family made a report at the Fiscalia and were provided with a protection order and phone numbers to get in direct contact with the police and advised to exercise self-protection measures. The Appellants temporarily relocated to stay with family in a different part of Medellin.

[5] The Appellants felt their case was not being taken seriously by the police, so they decided to seek asylum in Canada during their already-planned trip in XXXX 2018. On December 8, 2018, two men approached their mother-in-law who lived in a different suburb of Medellin and inquired about XXXX. She attempted to add this new incident to the previous report with the Fiscalia, although due to a holiday and the fact they already had made a complaint in their home area, she was unable to do so until XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018. The same day, the Appellants travelled to Canada.

[6] All the Appellants rely on the events involving XXXX and have made no other claims.

[7] The Appellants are not presenting new evidence nor seeking an oral hearing.

Evidence spans paragraphs 13-19. This is a deterministic evidence summary, not a legal conclusion.
subthemes.text:
[10] There is a presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens except in the case of a complete collapse.2 To rebut the presumption of state protection, the appellant must demonstrate the state's inability to protect its citizens with relevant, reliable and convincing evidence.3 Where a state has effective control of its territory, has military and police forces and established civilian authorities, and is making serious efforts to protect its citizens, the mere fact that it is not always successful in doing so is not sufficient to rebut the presumption.4 In addition, the burden of proof on the appellant increases with the degree of democracy achieved in the state in question. The more democratic a state is, the more the appellant will have to seek to use the available remedies to demonstrate that state protection was not available.5 The test for state protection is forward-looking, meaning whether there is evidence to establish that the state will be willing or able to provide protection in the future.6

[11] The Appellants contacted the police after the first contact with XXXX. They were given a protection order and multiple ways to contact the police. They left the country less than 20 days from the first contact and two days after the second contact. The Appellants argue that the RPD incorrectly faulted them for leaving on XXXX XXXX, the same day that their mother-in-law completed a complaint to the Fiscalia. I agree with the Appellants that the mother-in-law, being the person to whom the second threats were communicated, was an appropriate person to make this second complaint. For that reason, I agree that the RPD was incorrect to state that the mother-in-law was not involved in the incident. I also find that the fact that the gang followed the Appellants to a family member's home in a separate location is troubling. However, I find that a negative inference can be drawn about the parents' failure to accompany their mother-in-law to complete the complaint and their failure to follow up on the complaint. In my view, these actions show that the family did not take all objectively reasonable efforts to exhaust all courses of action reasonably available to them in Colombia. As the Federal Court has noted, "In the absence of a compelling or persuasive explanation, a failure to take reasonable steps to exhaust all courses of action reasonably available ... (does) not displace the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence."7 I find that the Appellants' decision to leave Colombia after one incident and to fail to follow up with the state agencies are not a compelling or persuasive explanation.

[12] The Appellants also argue that the measures taken by the state authorities were inadequate. Those measures included an order from the Fiscalia to the local police to provide protection to the Appellants, cellular telephone numbers to directly contact the police in the event of another incident and advice on self-protection measures. Immediately after their first complaint, the Appellants were given an order for police protection, showing that the state agreed with the seriousness of their complaint and took immediate action. The Appellants were given recommendations to change their routines, avoid poorly lit areas, not opening their doors to strangers, installing protection measures at their home, etc.8 The police also responded to the Fiscalia's protection order by giving the Appellants the names and numbers of police officers to get rapid and direct access to police officers. The Appellants testified that police refused to take additional measures unless XXXX was contacted again or physically threatened. The Appellants argue that all of these measures would be "after the fact" which would be inadequate given the media reports of retaliatory and violent criminal gangs. I disagree with this assessment of the adequacy of the state protection measures: the measures proposed by the police are common preventative protection which are counselled to victims of crimes. Curiously, the Appellants have provided a news article showing the Gulf Clan had declared a holiday ceasefire from December 8, 2018, to January 10, 2019.9 This article reinforces that state protection was adequate during the period immediately following the second incident. I find that the state protection measures were adequate and effective.

[13] In this finding, I am also guided by the Federal Court who has indicated that a subjective perception of the ineffectiveness of police action does not constitute compelling or persuasive evidence of inadequate state protection.10 Federal Court decisions recognize that state projection may not always be perfect, but it must be effectively extended to the claimants. 11 In considering that the caselaw requires that the protection be adequate and not perfect,12 I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the police's decision not to provide other measures unless there was a second incident does not establish that the state protection is not ineffective.

[14] I also note that the Appellants benefitted from four state programs to provide protection and reparations for victims of crime: a report to police of a single incident13; an application for national police protection measure;14 an order for police protection;15 an order from the Ombudsman Office of Colombia;16 and registration with Victims Unit.17

[15] Finally, the Appellants argue that the RPD ignored the country condition evidence of the inadequacy of state protection. They provided the RPD with 30 articles discussing youth recruitment, the FARC, street gangs in Medellin and gang violence. I find that several of these articles deal with situations which are not relevant to the Appellants' situation such as actions against human rights defenders,18 actions taken by the FARC or FARC dissidents19 or action in other geographic areas.20

[16] In reviewing the Appellant's memoranda, the articles they provided to the RPD and the country condition evidence, I agree that the country condition evidence shows that the Gulf Clan is one of the largest and most dangerous paramilitary groups in Colombia.21 The 2015 UNHCR guidelines from 2015 also found that "the Los Urabe±os are reported to have nation-wide networks with other armed groups and are able to trace and target individuals anywhere in the country."22 While there is no mention of the Los Chivos in the country condition evidence, it shows that the Gulf Clan uses local criminal groups to create these networks.23 The articles provided by the Appellants indicate that there are several paramilitary groups in Medellin and more than 240 different street gangs. 24 One article mentions the Los Chivos gang operating in the suburb where they lived25 although another article seems to imply the Los Chivos are not allied with the Gulf Cartel.26

subthemes.text:
[17] In regards to the adequacy of state protection, the Appellants' evidence and country condition evidence shows that violence and civil unrest continues to be a problem in Colombia such as the emergence of large criminal cartels taking over the former FARC activities, the continued presence of paramilitary groups, large communities of internally displaced people, forced disappearances, significant drug production and export.27 The evidence shows that the government is making significant efforts to deal with past corruption and interference with prosecutions.28 The evidence also shows that the rates of homicide, subversion and domestic terrorism continue to fall.29 The evidence shows that Colombia has instituted programs, financial and human resources and legislation to provide protection to civilians and reparations to victims of armed conflict as well as evidence of failures in these efforts, such as assassinations of social leaders.30 I have carefully reviewed the information about the effectiveness of these measures and find that these measures are not perfect, but met the standard for adequate state protection.31 Having reviewed the objective evidence and the country conditions evidence provided by the Appellant, I find that there is evidence of adequate state protection.

[18] I find that the Appellants have failed to rebut the presumption of state protection and have not met their burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or that they would personally be subjected to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture if they returned to Colombia.

discussion_units.text:
[17] In regards to the adequacy of state protection, the Appellants' evidence and country condition evidence shows that violence and civil unrest continues to be a problem in Colombia such as the emergence of large criminal cartels taking over the former FARC activities, the continued presence of paramilitary groups, large communities of internally displaced people, forced disappearances, significant drug production and export.27 The evidence shows that the government is making significant efforts to deal with past corruption and interference with prosecutions.28 The evidence also shows that the rates of homicide, subversion and domestic terrorism continue to fall.29 The evidence shows that Colombia has instituted programs, financial and human resources and legislation to provide protection to civilians and reparations to victims of armed conflict as well as evidence of failures in these efforts, such as assassinations of social leaders.30 I have carefully reviewed the information about the effectiveness of these measures and find that these measures are not perfect, but met the standard for adequate state protection.31 Having reviewed the objective evidence and the country conditions evidence provided by the Appellant, I find that there is evidence of adequate state protection.

[18] I find that the Appellants have failed to rebut the presumption of state protection and have not met their burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or that they would personally be subjected to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture if they returned to Colombia.

REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW

[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant), XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX are citizens of Colombia. They are a family of a wife, husband, and three adult children. The family fears a criminal cartel who tried to recruit the youngest child in November 2018. The family made a complaint to the Fiscalia and the Ombudsman, registered with the Victims Unit and were provided with a protection order. The family claimed refugee protection during a pre-planned trip to Canada in December 2018. The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) found that the determinative issue was state protection. I agree that this is the determinative issue.
DECISION
[2] I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
BACKGROUND

[3] The Appellants resided in a quiet suburb of Medellin. The family suspected that gang members would sometimes pass through the neighbourhood to reach nearby high-crime areas. XXXX was actively involved in young leadership programs in his school and community. He is also a talented XXXX who would perform publicly.

[4] In October 2018 the family planned a vacation to Canada for XXXX 2018. On November 20, 2018, an unknown young man visited the family's home and tried to recruit XXXX to the Los Chivos gang. He refused. The young man said he would return and threatened XXXX not to tell his parents. The family made a report at the Fiscalia and were provided with a protection order and phone numbers to get in direct contact with the police and advised to exercise self-protection measures. The Appellants temporarily relocated to stay with family in a different part of Medellin.

[5] The Appellants felt their case was not being taken seriously by the police, so they decided to seek asylum in Canada during their already-planned trip in XXXX 2018. On December 8, 2018, two men approached their mother-in-law who lived in a different suburb of Medellin and inquired about XXXX. She attempted to add this new incident to the previous report with the Fiscalia, although due to a holiday and the fact they already had made a complaint in their home area, she was unable to do so until XXXX XXXX XXXX 2018. The same day, the Appellants travelled to Canada.
[6] All the Appellants rely on the events involving XXXX and have made no other claims.
[7] The Appellants are not presenting new evidence nor seeking an oral hearing.
ANALYSIS

[8] My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.1
State Protection

[9] Refugee protection is meant to be a form of surrogate protection, to be invoked only in those situations where the refugee claimant has unsuccessfully sought the protection of their home state. The onus is on the refugee claimant to approach the state for protection in situations where state protection might be reasonably forthcoming.

[10] There is a presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens except in the case of a complete collapse.2 To rebut the presumption of state protection, the appellant must demonstrate the state's inability to protect its citizens with relevant, reliable and convincing evidence.3 Where a state has effective control of its territory, has military and police forces and established civilian authorities, and is making serious efforts to protect its citizens, the mere fact that it is not always successful in doing so is not sufficient to rebut the presumption.4 In addition, the burden of proof on the appellant increases with the degree of democracy achieved in the state in question. The more democratic a state is, the more the appellant will have to seek to use the available remedies to demonstrate that state protection was not available.5 The test for state protection is forward-looking, meaning whether there is evidence to establish that the state will be willing or able to provide protection in the future.6

[11] The Appellants contacted the police after the first contact with XXXX. They were given a protection order and multiple ways to contact the police. They left the country less than 20 days from the first contact and two days after the second contact. The Appellants argue that the RPD incorrectly faulted them for leaving on XXXX XXXX, the same day that their mother-in-law completed a complaint to the Fiscalia. I agree with the Appellants that the mother-in-law, being the person to whom the second threats were communicated, was an appropriate person to make this second complaint. For that reason, I agree that the RPD was incorrect to state that the mother-in-law was not involved in the incident. I also find that the fact that the gang followed the Appellants to a family member's home in a separate location is troubling. However, I find that a negative inference can be drawn about the parents' failure to accompany their mother-in-law to complete the complaint and their failure to follow up on the complaint. In my view, these actions show that the family did not take all objectively reasonable efforts to exhaust all courses of action reasonably available to them in Colombia. As the Federal Court has noted, "In the absence of a compelling or persuasive explanation, a failure to take reasonable steps to exhaust all courses of action reasonably available ... (does) not displace the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence."7 I find that the Appellants' decision to leave Colombia after one incident and to fail to follow up with the state agencies are not a compelling or persuasive explanation.

[12] The Appellants also argue that the measures taken by the state authorities were inadequate. Those measures included an order from the Fiscalia to the local police to provide protection to the Appellants, cellular telephone numbers to directly contact the police in the event of another incident and advice on self-protection measures. Immediately after their first complaint, the Appellants were given an order for police protection, showing that the state agreed with the seriousness of their complaint and took immediate action. The Appellants were given recommendations to change their routines, avoid poorly lit areas, not opening their doors to strangers, installing protection measures at their home, etc.8 The police also responded to the Fiscalia's protection order by giving the Appellants the names and numbers of police officers to get rapid and direct access to police officers. The Appellants testified that police refused to take additional measures unless XXXX was contacted again or physically threatened. The Appellants argue that all of these measures would be "after the fact" which would be inadequate given the media reports of retaliatory and violent criminal gangs. I disagree with this assessment of the adequacy of the state protection measures: the measures proposed by the police are common preventative protection which are counselled to victims of crimes. Curiously, the Appellants have provided a news article showing the Gulf Clan had declared a holiday ceasefire from December 8, 2018, to January 10, 2019.9 This article reinforces that state protection was adequate during the period immediately following the second incident. I find that the state protection measures were adequate and effective.

[13] In this finding, I am also guided by the Federal Court who has indicated that a subjective perception of the ineffectiveness of police action does not constitute compelling or persuasive evidence of inadequate state protection.10 Federal Court decisions recognize that state projection may not always be perfect, but it must be effectively extended to the claimants. 11 In considering that the caselaw requires that the protection be adequate and not perfect,12 I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the police's decision not to provide other measures unless there was a second incident does not establish that the state protection is not ineffective.

[14] I also note that the Appellants benefitted from four state programs to provide protection and reparations for victims of crime: a report to police of a single incident13; an application for national police protection measure;14 an order for police protection;15 an order from the Ombudsman Office of Colombia;16 and registration with Victims Unit.17

[15] Finally, the Appellants argue that the RPD ignored the country condition evidence of the inadequacy of state protection. They provided the RPD with 30 articles discussing youth recruitment, the FARC, street gangs in Medellin and gang violence. I find that several of these articles deal with situations which are not relevant to the Appellants' situation such as actions against human rights defenders,18 actions taken by the FARC or FARC dissidents19 or action in other geographic areas.20

[16] In reviewing the Appellant's memoranda, the articles they provided to the RPD and the country condition evidence, I agree that the country condition evidence shows that the Gulf Clan is one of the largest and most dangerous paramilitary groups in Colombia.21 The 2015 UNHCR guidelines from 2015 also found that "the Los Urabe±os are reported to have nation-wide networks with other armed groups and are able to trace and target individuals anywhere in the country."22 While there is no mention of the Los Chivos in the country condition evidence, it shows that the Gulf Clan uses local criminal groups to create these networks.23 The articles provided by the Appellants indicate that there are several paramilitary groups in Medellin and more than 240 different street gangs. 24 One article mentions the Los Chivos gang operating in the suburb where they lived25 although another article seems to imply the Los Chivos are not allied with the Gulf Cartel.26

[17] In regards to the adequacy of state protection, the Appellants' evidence and country condition evidence shows that violence and civil unrest continues to be a problem in Colombia such as the emergence of large criminal cartels taking over the former FARC activities, the continued presence of paramilitary groups, large communities of internally displaced people, forced disappearances, significant drug production and export.27 The evidence shows that the government is making significant efforts to deal with past corruption and interference with prosecutions.28 The evidence also shows that the rates of homicide, subversion and domestic terrorism continue to fall.29 The evidence shows that Colombia has instituted programs, financial and human resources and legislation to provide protection to civilians and reparations to victims of armed conflict as well as evidence of failures in these efforts, such as assassinations of social leaders.30 I have carefully reviewed the information about the effectiveness of these measures and find that these measures are not perfect, but met the standard for adequate state protection.31 Having reviewed the objective evidence and the country conditions evidence provided by the Appellant, I find that there is evidence of adequate state protection.

[18] I find that the Appellants have failed to rebut the presumption of state protection and have not met their burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or that they would personally be subjected to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture if they returned to Colombia.
CONCLUSION

[19] Pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Act, I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
(signed)
Pamela Arnott
Pamela Arnott
